findings.title: Fail closed when the installation has no local Integration row
findings.body: The Integration.DoesNotExist branch advances without comparing the OAuth user to the installation's sender. GitHub installation webhooks are asynchronous and can fail, so a valid installation can exist on GitHub without a local Integration row. An attacker authenticated with their own GitHub account can supply that installation ID and reach build_integration, which uses app credentials to fetch and attach it to the attacker's Sentry organization. Obtain trusted authorization data or reject the request when the local verification data is unavailable instead of skipping verification.

findings.title: Compare immutable GitHub user IDs instead of logins
findings.body: The authenticated identity stores only GitHub's login, which is subsequently compared with the login cached in the installation's sender metadata. GitHub usernames can change, and old usernames can be claimed by another account. After an installer renames their account, the legitimate installer fails verification while someone who acquires the former username can pass it and claim an unlinked installation. Store the authenticated user's immutable numeric ID and compare it with sender.id instead.

findings.title: Handle installations without sender metadata
findings.body: This comparison unconditionally accesses integration.metadata['sender']['login'], but build_integration only includes sender when it is present in pipeline state, and the new OAuth/UI flow never binds that state field. Consequently, active Integration records created through that flow can lack sender metadata. If such a record remains without an OrganizationIntegration, reconnecting it raises KeyError and produces a server error instead of the intended verification-failure page. Handle missing sender data explicitly and fail closed or recover trusted installer information.

findings.title: Keep the missing-installation test on the GitHub 404 path
findings.body: The GitHub-404 handling in build_integration is unchanged and still raises 'The GitHub installation could not be found.' This test now expects 'Invalid installation request.' instead, so a passing test validates an earlier OAuth rejection rather than the stubbed installation 404. The installation lookup can disappear entirely without this test detecting it. Use the state returned by the authorization redirect, assert that the installation request occurs, and retain the not-found message assertion to preserve coverage of the original error path.
